title: Love God, Serve Man -- Ch. 14: Investment Prospects in Philippine Tourism
keywords: Paoay Lake Golf and Sports Complex
primary_topics: Chapter 14 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- CJP's briefing of February 28, 1988 at the Manila Garden Hotel, delivered at the request of the Philippine-Chinese Business Council to visiting Taiwanese businessmen assessing investment possibilities in Philippine tourism.

The case that the Philippine investment climate is attractive: businessmen's restored confidence, attractive government incentives, and a stabilized peace and order situation, supported by Board of Investments figures showing P30.97 billion invested in 1988, 160 percent above 1987.

The specific fiscal and non-fiscal incentives available to tourism investors under the Omnibus Investments Code of 1987, the Investment Priorities Plan, and Executive Order No. 63 -- income tax holidays, duty-free capital equipment, labor-expense deductions, residence and repatriation rights for aliens investing at least US$50,000.

The state of Philippine tourism and its investment openings: a first million visitor arrivals worth over $1.5 billion, DOT programs and targets, a quantified shortage of hotel rooms, vehicles and airline seats requiring some $300 million in new investment, and the government hotels and resorts then up for sale or lease.
sub_topics: He opens by calling 1988 'a banner year of economic achievements,' with real GNP growing 7 percent against a 5.7 percent target, and lists three reasons the investment climate is attractive: investor confidence, government incentives, and stabilized peace and order.

Confidence in figures: BOI statistics show P30.97 billion ($1.475 billion) invested in 1988, 160 percent above the P11.9 billion of 1987 and 47.5 percent past the P21-billion target; foreign investment eclipsed 1987 by 70.1 percent and was nearly three times the 1986 figure.

The headline tourism deal: some $80 million from Singapore-based Shangri-la Hotel Corporation for a 600-room, 20-story hotel on Ortigas in Mandaluyong and a bigger one in the Ayala Commercial Center in Makati; the Japanese led investors that year, followed by the British and the Americans.

Why activity should stay upbeat: appreciating Asian currencies push investors overseas in search of cheap manufacturing, and a recent Philippine Investors' Forum reached consensus on pushing through 71 projects worth $234 million in 1989 and 1990.

The 1988 Investment Priorities Plan identifies 277 areas entitled to incentives under the Omnibus Investments Code, described by Trade and Industry Secretary Jose S. Concepcion Jr. as 'the vehicle to direct investments into those areas where the country's need is greatest,' and reflecting the BOI's shift to 'a promotional, rather than regulatory, regime.'

The Omnibus Investments Code of 1987 aligns Philippine incentives with those of other ASEAN countries and adds an income tax holiday for preferred areas, a deduction for additional direct labor expense, and private sector representation on the BOI board.

Six fiscal incentives for BOI-registered tourism enterprises -- a four-year income tax holiday (six for pioneer firms), duty-free importation of capital equipment, tax credit on domestic equipment, additional labor-expense deduction, bonded warehouse access, and exemption from the contractor's tax -- plus three non-fiscal ones: simplified customs, unrestricted use of consigned equipment, and employment of foreign nationals in supervisory, technical or advisory posts.
Projects in less developed areas automatically get pioneer incentives, and the cost of necessary major infrastructure and public utilities may be deducted from taxable income in full.

Executive Order No. 63 grants any alien investing at least US$50,000 in a tourist project residence for himself, his wife and unmarried minor children for as long as the investment subsists, the right to remit earnings and repatriate liquidation proceeds in the original currency, and the same privileges to his surviving family.

Tourism's own numbers: the country passed the one-million mark in visitor arrivals against an 860,000 target, which Tourism Secretary Jose Antonio Gonzalez estimated at over $1.5 billion in foreign exchange, with targets of 1.2 million for 1989 and 1.5 million for 1991.

President Corazon C. Aquino's personal interest produced the DOT's five-year Fiesta Island Program aimed at foreign and domestic tourists, the Balik Fiesta Program for overseas Filipinos, invitations to American veterans under Proclamation No. 130's Pacific War Veterans Homecoming Period, and positioning of the country as an incentive destination.

The selling points: spectacular natural beauty, hospitable people (almost 60 percent of 1988 tourists were repeat visitors), an American newsmagazine writer's line about smiles, and value -- 'the Philippines is the best bargain in Asia.'

The capacity gap: to serve more than two million tourists by 1991 the country needs 7,000 de luxe, 1,300 first-class and 3,000 standard hotel rooms, plus 1,000 tourist-inn rooms, 1,000 apartelle rooms, 700 pension rooms and 12,245 resort rooms, 1,400 rental cars, 1,144 coach seats and 521,102 additional airline seats a year -- some $300 million in new investment.

Improved peace and order: the Department of National Defense reported six 'firsts' for 1988, from capturing the most CPP/NPA/NDF leaders since 1976 to reversing the combat fatalities, firearms losses and tactical initiative ratios.

Concrete openings: government hotels still to be auctioned -- Manila Hotel, Philippine Plaza and Puerto Azul -- plus six properties for sale or lease, from Fort Ilocandia and the Paoay Lake Golf and Sports Complex in Ilocos Norte to Banaue, Mt. Data, Marbella Marina and the Leyte Park Hotel, each with its location, travel time and facilities described.

The close: after the decline of 1981 to 1985, tourism shows 'an unmistakable upswing in arrivals, investments and returns,' offers 'a very short incubation period for profits,' and so 'The wise entrepreneur will not wait for tomorrow. He will invest NOW.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 14 of 'Love God, Serve Man' is the briefing CJP gave at the Manila Garden Hotel, at the request of the Philippine-Chinese Business Council, to Taiwanese businessmen assessing tourism investments in the Philippines. He opened by calling 1988 'a banner year of economic achievements,' citing 7 percent real GNP growth against a 5.7 percent target, and gave three reasons the climate was attractive: investor confidence, government incentives, and a stabilized peace and order situation. Board of Investments figures carried the first point -- P30.97 billion invested in 1988, 160 percent above 1987 and 47.5 percent past target, with foreign capital nearly triple the 1986 level, the Japanese leading, and Singapore-based Shangri-la committing some $80 million to new hotels in Mandaluyong and Makati. For incentives he walked through the 1988 Investment Priorities Plan's 277 preferred areas, described by Secretary Jose S. Concepcion Jr. as 'the vehicle to direct investments into those areas where the country's need is greatest'; the Omnibus Investments Code of 1987, aligned with ASEAN practice; six fiscal and three non-fiscal incentives for BOI-registered tourism enterprises; automatic pioneer status for less developed areas; and Executive Order No. 63, which gives any alien investing US$50,000 or more residence for his family, remittance of earnings and repatriation of proceeds. He then reported tourism's own numbers -- the first million arrivals, over $1.5 billion in foreign exchange, targets of 1.2 million for 1989 and 1.5 million for 1991, President Aquino's personal interest, and the DOT's Fiesta Island and Balik Fiesta programs -- and quantified the shortfall of rooms, rental cars, coach and airline seats requiring roughly $300 million in new investment. After citing the defense department's six 'firsts' against the insurgency, he listed the government hotels and resorts still for sale or lease, from Manila Hotel to Leyte Park, and closed that the wise entrepreneur would not wait for tomorrow but invest now.
